title: Type-Level Testing and Documentation
learning_outcomes: Explain positive and negative type tests in the context of type-level testing and documentation.
Apply the lesson concept in a small TypeScript example and describe what the compiler can check.
Identify one limitation or failure case and choose an appropriate runtime check or test when needed.

content.intro: Learn type-level testing and documentation through a compact mental model, syllabus-aligned subtopics, a worked example and a practical task. The goal is not to memorize syntax but to know what the type contract guarantees and what evidence is still needed.
content.why_it_matters: Model the narrowest honest type contract. Prefer inference where it is clear, use unknown at untrusted boundaries, and use control-flow checks before performing operations that depend on a value’s shape.

content_blocks.title: Mental model
content_blocks.text: **Type-Level Testing and Documentation.** This lesson belongs to **Advanced Type System**. Start by identifying the problem that type-level testing and documentation solves. In TypeScript, separate three questions: what values your program intends to accept, what the compiler can prove from the code, and what must still be checked while the program runs. The last category matters whenever data comes from a user, file, API, storage layer, or an untyped JavaScript dependency.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics and how to use them

items.title: Positive and negative type tests
items.text: For positive and negative type tests, define observable acceptance criteria and test both expected behavior and a failure case. Preserve a small regression test for any bug or inference problem you fix.

items.title: Testing inferred types
items.text: For testing inferred types, define observable acceptance criteria and test both expected behavior and a failure case. Preserve a small regression test for any bug or inference problem you fix.

items.title: Documenting complex generic APIs
items.text: For documenting complex generic apis, treat incoming values as untrusted until runtime checks establish the required shape. A TypeScript annotation does not validate network, file, database, storage, or user-provided data by itself.

content_blocks.title: Example: Type-Level Testing and Documentation
content_blocks.expected_output: UserKey resolves to "id" | "active". Type-level examples are checked by a TypeScript compiler, not a JavaScript runtime.

content_blocks.title: Compile-time versus runtime
content_blocks.text: Type annotations and most type declarations are erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript. They do not validate external JSON, authorize a user, sanitize HTML, or prevent runtime failures by themselves. Validate trust-boundary inputs and test the behavior.

content.task: Create a small TypeScript example for “Type-Level Testing and Documentation”. Demonstrate positive and negative type tests, explain your assumption, and include one check that shows the expected behavior. Do not treat a type annotation as runtime validation for external input.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one syllabus subtopic named in this lesson.
The type contract is explicit enough that another learner can explain what it accepts and rejects.
The learner records a failure case and distinguishes compile-time checks from runtime validation.
hints: Start with the syllabus item “Positive and negative type tests” and define the smallest example that demonstrates it.
Ask which part is checked by TypeScript and which part depends on runtime data, the environment or a test.
For external input, start with unknown and validate the required shape before using a domain type.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a successful type check as a runtime guarantee.
common_mistakes.why: Type annotations do not generally validate data after JavaScript starts running.
common_mistakes.fix: Add runtime checks for external input and tests for meaningful failure cases.

common_mistakes.problem: Using any or an assertion to silence a useful diagnostic.
common_mistakes.why: That can hide the exact mismatch the type system would otherwise report.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer a more precise type or unknown plus narrowing; use assertions only when a verified invariant justifies them.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a compiler setting or runtime example without checking the project environment.
common_mistakes.why: Module resolution, DOM/Node globals, JSX and tool behavior depend on the configured versions and environment.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin the toolchain, match tsconfig to the runtime/bundler, and run the actual project's typecheck and tests.

summary: Type-Level Testing and Documentation is taught through the subtopics listed in the source syllabus: Positive and negative type tests, Testing inferred types, Documenting complex generic APIs.
Prefer precise contracts and use compiler diagnostics as evidence, not as a replacement for runtime tests.
Validate untrusted data and describe environment/version assumptions explicitly.
